claims.claim: deer crop aquatic plants in late spring and early summer, most when water is low, but the aquatic share of their diet is 'unknown but probably low'
claims.source_value: the source reads 'The portion of the diet that aquatic vegetation comprises during periods of peak use is unknown but is probably low' — the paper's quotation drops the second 'is' and the qualifier 'during periods of peak use'
claims.location: p. 2 (PDF p. 2), 'Seasonal foods of deer in the Upper Great Lakes Region'
claims.quote: peak use is unknown but is probably low
claims.conditions: a review of Upper Great Lakes (Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan) studies; the aquatic-feeding statements come from cited studies (Hennings 1977 in north-eastern Minnesota; Joyal & Scherrer 1978; Townsend & Smith 1933 and others); deer 'are sometimes observed eating aquatic vegetation', and 'Aquatic feeding reaches its peak during periods of reduced water levels in early summer'
claims.note: The facts check (late spring–early summer, peak at low water, share probably low); fix the quotation to 'unknown but is probably low', or paraphrase without quotation marks.

claims.claim: deer feed at the water in 'late spring and early summer' (mapped to late May – early August, an inference)
claims.quote: In late spring and early summer, deer, like moose
claims.conditions: Upper Great Lakes review; the calendar mapping is the project's

notes: Hennings (1977, cited p. 2) saw deer in north-eastern Minnesota select, in decreasing order, burreeds, filamentous algae, ribbonleaf pondweed, water horsetail, arrowhead, sedges, marsh cinquefoil, white and yellow pond lilies, purple watershield and St. John's-wort; water milfoil and wild rice are also reported. Aquatic plants may supply sodium (p. 2). The review notes that the feeding-site examination method misses aquatic feeding entirely (p. 5), one reason the aquatic share is unknown.
